Why the Nucleus

ATAK is only as good as the network under it. Cell coverage disappears, and standing up infrastructure takes time a team in the field does not have. Without a network, everyone is back to radio calls and guesswork.

The Nucleus is a portable, battery-powered mesh radio that brings its own network. A high-speed WiFi mesh carries full IP traffic, so anything that runs over a normal network runs over the mesh, ATAK situational awareness, voice, video, and file transfer included. A separate long-range LoRa radio carries position and chat far past WiFi range. Nodes find each other automatically, route around failures, and need no base station. Any node with an internet connection shares it with the rest of the mesh.

Everything below is measured outdoors in live field conditions. No lab results, no simulations.

12.26 kmLoRa with no packet loss

Performance Summary

Each row below is a separate field test. Full detail for each follows in the next section.

Test Conditions WiFi result LoRa result
Open water, elevated node Base node 48 m above water, clear line of sight Mesh link established at approximately 5,500 m on the return heading, the longest WiFi link measured to date. Approximately 4 Mbps sustained between 2 km and 2.5 km. Outbound on a different heading the link held to approximately 1,600 m at 2.9 Mbps No loss out to 12.26 km, the limit of the test area
Apartment complex, no line of sight Ground level, multi-story buildings between nodes Blocked by approximately 75 m No loss across the entire complex, 250 m and beyond
Open field, clear line of sight Both nodes at approximately 4 ft elevation Below 1 Mbps at 800 m, link held at 900 m, lost between 900 m and 1 km Not tested
Mixed terrain, three nodes Ground level, forced multi-hop path Good throughput to approximately 300 m clear, link lost beyond approximately 500 m obstructed Not tested
Obstructed terrain, two nodes Ground level, heavier obstruction than above Approximately 1 Mbps by 300 m, dropouts from 350 m, mostly lost by 400 m Not tested
Reading these numbers. WiFi range is governed almost entirely by line of sight and antenna elevation, not by distance alone. Antennas close to the ground also lose signal to ground reflection, which is why a node placed high performs far better than the same node at chest height. The same hardware linked at 5.5 km over open water from an elevated position and 75 m through a building. LoRa range is far less sensitive to obstruction and provides a fallback path when the WiFi mesh cannot reach.

Field Test Detail

1. Maximum Range, Open Water with Elevation

This test measures maximum achievable range under highly favorable conditions. LoRa was checked across the full extent of the test area.

Setup

A stationary node was staged approximately 48 m above a lake, with its Meshtastic radio placed in range test mode. A second node was carried by boat onto the lake. The WiFi link was tracked from the mobile node's web interface, and the mobile node's Meshtastic radio logged sequential pings from the base node.

Results

  • Outbound, WiFi throughput fell from 5.7 Mbps to approximately 2.9 Mbps at around 1,600 m, then dropped out entirely before 1,700 m.
  • LoRa pings continued without failure out to 12.26 km, at which point the test ended because the lake ended.
  • On the return leg, on a slightly different heading, the WiFi mesh re-established at approximately 5,500 m. Throughput then improved with decreasing distance, reaching approximately 4 Mbps between 2 km and 2.5 km.
  • A throughput dip near 500 m is attributed to terrain shadowing between the base node and the dock.

Analysis

With height and unobstructed line of sight, the WiFi mesh operates at kilometer scale. The difference between the 1,600 m outbound cutoff and the 5,500 m return reacquisition on a slightly different heading shows how sensitive the WiFi link is to the specific path, even over open water.

2. Combined WiFi and LoRa Performance, Congested Urban Area

This test measures both networks in a built-up residential area with no line of sight and no intermediate relay nodes.

Setup

The stationary node was connected to an external antenna on a second story balcony. The mobile node used stock antennas and was carried in a pack. The site was an apartment complex of large units built in 2014.

Both Meshtastic radios were disconnected from the node serial link and placed in range test mode using the official application, with the stationary node transmitting on a 15 second cycle. The mobile node was then walked throughout the complex. WiFi link quality was recorded at each location from the node web interface. Once WiFi was lost, LoRa pings continued to be logged.

Results

  • With no intermediate node to restore line of sight, a single large apartment building was sufficient to block the WiFi mesh by approximately 75 m.
  • LoRa held a connection across the entire complex, out to 250 m and beyond, with no dropped pings for the full duration of the test.

Analysis

This is the worst case for the WiFi mesh and a straightforward case for LoRa. In this type of environment, useful WiFi coverage depends on placing additional nodes to maintain line of sight between hops. LoRa continues to carry situational awareness and chat regardless.

3. WiFi Range, Open Field with Clear Line of Sight

Setup

  • Open field, clear line of sight.
  • Two nodes with standard antennas, both at approximately 4 ft elevation.
  • One node stationary, one mounted on an off-highway vehicle.

Results

  • WiFi data rate fell below 1 Mbps at 800 m.
  • The link was still established at 900 m.
  • The link was lost between 900 m and 1 km.

Why elevation matters

At 2.4 GHz, part of the signal reaches the far node after bouncing off the ground. That reflected copy arrives slightly out of phase with the direct signal and cancels some of it. The effect gets worse the closer the antennas sit to the ground, and it happens even with a completely clear view between nodes, so it is not obstruction in the usual sense.

The rough rule of thumb is that a 900 m link at this frequency wants somewhere around 10 ft of antenna height to stay clear of the ground reflection, and a 5 km link wants closer to 25 ft. Both nodes in this test were at about 4 ft. These are approximate figures rather than measurements, but they line up reasonably well with what we saw: throughput went marginal past 800 m and the link died before 1 km.

The practical takeaway is that the 900 m figure here is a floor set by antenna height, not a limit of the radio. Getting one node onto a mast, rooftop, vehicle mount, or high ground is the single most effective change available. Test 1 is the same hardware with the base node 48 m up, and it linked at 5.5 km.

Analysis

At ground level with clear line of sight, usable WiFi range approaches 1 km, but throughput becomes marginal well before the link drops. As noted above, this is driven largely by antenna height rather than the distance itself.

4. WiFi Throughput Against Range, Three Nodes

Setup

  • Varying terrain and obstacles.
  • Three nodes with standard antennas.
  • Node 1 mobile at approximately 4 ft, node 3 fixed at approximately 4 ft, node 2 at ground level near clutter but with line of sight to node 3, in order to force multi-hop behavior.

Results

  • Good throughput maintained to approximately 300 m with clear line of sight.
  • Trees blocking direct line of sight reduced maximum range to approximately 500 m.
  • Throughput fell sharply beyond approximately 300 m.
  • The link was lost entirely beyond approximately 500 m when obstructed.

5. WiFi Throughput, Heavily Obstructed Terrain

Setup

  • Heavier line of sight obstruction than test 4.
  • Two nodes with standard antennas, both at approximately 4 ft elevation, connected directly.

Results

  • Throughput fell to approximately 1 Mbps by 300 m once line of sight was obstructed.
  • Dropouts became noticeable at 350 m.
  • The link was mostly lost by 400 m.
  • Across a section from 250 m to 320 m with relatively clear line of sight, only a mild throughput reduction was observed.
  • Introducing obstruction from 320 m to 370 m produced a severe throughput reduction.

Analysis

Obstruction, rather than raw distance, is the dominant limit on both throughput and link stability. The drop-off when line of sight is broken is far sharper than the gradual decline seen in clear conditions.

Expected Performance by Environment

Environment WiFi mesh LoRa
Clear line of sight with elevation Up to 5.5 km demonstrated over open water from 48 m elevation. Approximately 3 to 6 Mbps at long range, increasing as distance closes 12 km or more
Clear line of sight at ground level Up to approximately 900 m, with throughput below 1 Mbps past 800 m Multiple kilometers
Partially obstructed, vegetation Approximately 300 m at good throughput, up to approximately 500 m before loss Multiple kilometers
Heavily obstructed, buildings Approximately 75 m through a single large structure 250 m and beyond across a full apartment complex

Because the mesh is self-healing and multi-hop, additional nodes placed to maintain line of sight extend coverage well past any single link figure above. The per-link numbers describe one hop, not the reach of a deployed network.

Test Method and Limitations

  • All results were gathered outdoors in live field conditions. No laboratory, anechoic chamber, or simulated results are included.
  • WiFi link quality and throughput were read from the mesh routing statistics shown in the node web interface.
  • LoRa range was measured using the range test mode built into the Meshtastic firmware, logging sequential pings from a stationary transmitting node.
  • Except where stated, all tests used stock antennas as shipped. Test 2 used an external antenna on the stationary node only. No directional or high-gain antennas were used in any test, so the figures reflect the hardware as delivered rather than a tuned setup.
  • Distances are GPS derived.
  • Tests were conducted over a period of ongoing development. The mesh routing implementation has been revised since the earliest of these tests.
  • Radio performance depends heavily on terrain, obstruction, antenna height, and local spectrum congestion. These figures are representative of the conditions described and are not guaranteed for any other deployment.

What the Nucleus Solves

The sections above describe what the hardware is and how it measured in the field. This section describes what it is for. Each block below opens with the problem, then what the Nucleus does about it.

Two independent networks

Every Nucleus carries two radios that operate at the same time and do not depend on each other.

  • WiFi mesh. IEEE 802.11s on 2.4 GHz, encrypted with WPA3-SAE. It carries full IP traffic, so any application that runs over an ordinary network runs over it with no modification. Nodes discover each other, route through one another to extend reach, and re-route automatically when a node drops. Throughput reaches approximately 30 Mbps between nodes at close range and falls off with distance and obstruction, as detailed in the field test section above.
  • Meshtastic LoRa. An onboard radio running Meshtastic firmware. Throughput is very low, suitable for text and position rather than bulk data, but range is measured in kilometers and it holds through terrain and structures that stop WiFi outright.

Phones, tablets, and laptops join through the node's 5 GHz access point the same way they join any wireless network. No client software, no adapter, and no configuration on the end user device.

1. Texting

ProblemCoordinating a team means everyone is on a carrier. Step outside coverage and the group chat stops. Stay inside it and every message sent is sitting on infrastructure you do not own.

NucleusThree independent paths. Jami and Reticulum carry text over the WiFi mesh, and Meshtastic carries it over LoRa when nodes are too far apart for WiFi to reach. Reticulum applies strong encryption end to end. No carrier, no account, nothing to sign up for.

2. Voice and video

ProblemVoice and video calling depends entirely on cell towers. Lose coverage and it is gone. No calls, no video, no way to talk to the team beyond shouting distance or a handheld radio on an open channel.

NucleusGives it back to everyone on the mesh, two different ways.

Calls. Jami handles direct and group voice and video calls, encrypted, with no tower and no phone company involved. OpenDHT running on the nodes provides the peer discovery that would otherwise require a server, so calls work with no internet connection present.

Push to talk. A radio net for the whole mesh, built into the node software rather than bolted on as a separate app or a second piece of hardware. It runs over either network: WiFi for clear audio at mesh range, or LoRa to reach nodes that WiFi cannot. Audio goes in and out through the connected phone, or through a headset plugged straight into the node's exposed USB-C port, so a user can work handsfree with the phone stowed or not carry one at all.

3. Situational awareness

ProblemATAK is only as good as the network under it. Without one it is a map that shows you where you are and nothing about anyone else.

NucleusATAK runs natively over the WiFi mesh with no plugin required on the end user device. A CoT bridge on every node pushes position and chat over LoRa in parallel, so the shared picture holds well past the range WiFi can reach. Where a build includes an onboard TAKserver and MediaMTX, live video streaming is available to ATAK clients as well. TAKserver and MediaMTX are configured per build and are not present on every node.

4. Internet across the mesh

ProblemSometimes there is exactly one connection on site. A satellite terminal, a hotspot, an ethernet jack in a building. One connection, one device, and everyone else queues up behind it.

NucleusPlug that uplink into the ethernet port on any node and the connection is shared across the entire mesh. Every node and every connected device reaches the internet through it, and applications running on the nodes themselves get the same access.

5. Reach-back

ProblemA field team that can only talk to itself is still cut off. The TAKserver they need to be on is at headquarters, and the people who need to see the picture are not in the field.

NucleusWhere an internet uplink is available, Tailscale provides a secure IP tunnel from the mesh into the operator's own tailnet, reaching whatever is on it. A TAKserver at headquarters, a second mesh in another country, or any other infrastructure they run. Reticulum operates as a transport instance spanning both the local mesh and the internet link, extending encrypted Reticulum traffic beyond the deployment.

Across all of it

  • No infrastructure to stand up. No tower, no base station, no repeater, no central node.
  • No SIM, no carrier, and no subscription.
  • Battery powered and portable. Approximately 0.5 A at 5 V in normal operation, running from a standard USB power bank.
  • Nodes self-organize on power up and the mesh re-routes around a lost node without intervention.
  • The mesh is encrypted at the link layer with WPA3-SAE before any application traffic touches it.
  • A browser-based dashboard shows node status, link quality, throughput, and WiFi channel congestion, so nodes can be sited and checked without a laptop or a terminal.

Beyond all of the above, each node is a Linux computer with capacity to spare. The applications described here are a useful default set, not a fixed one, and additional services can be installed to suit a specific deployment.
